newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST- Financial Times - Monday, Feb 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST- Financial Times - Monday, Feb 17.

text.p: - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- WORLD TELECOMS PACT SET TO SLASH COST OF CALLS

The World Trade Organisation has secured commitments from almost 70 countries on a pact to liberalise telecommunications markets. The agreement, which will boost sales and investments in the $600 billion a year world market, could see the cost of international telephone calls fall by more than 80 per cent. Commenting on the accord, which was concluded late on Saturday, US trade representative Charlene Barshefsky said it was 'one of the most important trade agreements for the 21st Century'.
-- MOD MAY DELAY EUROFIGHTER MISSILE CONTRACT

The Ministry of Defence is considering postponing for a year a decision on whether to award a 900-million-stg missile contract to a European consortium led by British Aerospace or to a U.S. team led by Hughes. Such a delay could mean the Eurofighter aircraft is delivered to the Royal Air Force in 2002 before their main armament - the Medium Range Air-to-Air Missile - becomes available. The postonement option is being considered because of MoD uncertainty over aspects of designs from both bidders.
-- DISCOUNT GAS PRICES MAY BE FORCED UP

Gas industry executives are warning that companies currently offering customers discounts of up to 25 percent may have to raise their prices if the Monopolies and Mergers Commission does not agree with proposals from gas regulator Ofgas to cut gas transportation fees. A ruling from the MMC is due in April, but many of the independent gas companies who are offering low-price gas in areas where competition is allowed are thought to have based their prices on the Ofgas proposals being passed.
-- BRUSSELS TO SHAME EU STATES OVER SINGLE MARKET RULES

Mario Monti, the European Union's single market commissioner, is reported to be drawing up plans to publish a 'score board' of distortions to the single market in a bid to shame countries into complying with single-market rules. Member states will be scrutinised over a wide range of statistics, from levels of state aid to the number of complaints brought by people and businesses. The move comes amid concern that some member states are backsliding on single-market obligations in order to focus on preparations for economic and monetary union.
-- SHORTS TO ADD MORE JOBS THAN 1,000 LOST IN FOKKER COLLAPSE

Northern Ireland-based aerospace company Short Brothers is set to announce the creation of more than 1,000 jobs this week, substantially higher than the number of jobs lost at the firm last year after the collapse of Fokker of the Netherlands, one of Short's most important customers. The new jobs, details of which are expected to be revealed on Wednesday, will be created by new manufacturing contracts.
-- UK GROUP'S TOKYO MAN 'PAID HAMANAKA Y20M'

A BBC current affairs programme will on Monday night claim Yasuo Hamanaka, former chief copper trader of Japanese trading company Sumitomo Corp, received at least Y20 million (99,000 pounds sg) in cash from the Tokyo representative of a UK-based commodities trading group. The payments relate to what the programme claims was an 'unfairly priced' deal between Sumitomo and the UK group, Winchester Commodities. Hamanaka is on trail in Japan in connection with unauthorised copper trading that cost Sumitomo $2.6 billion.
-- TORIES CONSIDER TRADE ROLE FOR FOREIGN OFFICE

The Conservatives are reported to be considering radical plans to reduce and reform government departments, including transferring Britain's trade operation to the Foreign Office. Among the ideas being considered are an enhanced role for the environment department, with it possibly taking over most of the Agriculture Ministry or transport; transferring food safety from agriculture to health; and new responsibilities for the DTI, possibly transport or broadcasting.
-- ENTERPRISE PLANS FULL DEVELOPMENT OF ITALIAN OIL FIND

UK oil explorer Enterprise Oil has said it hopes to proceed soon to full-scale development of a find in the southern Apennines of Italy. The find is said to be one of western Europe's largest oil discoveries, and the impetus towards full development follows a technical breakthrough. Enterprise is confident that wells at the site will be able to produce up to 10,000 barrels a day each. Overall, the discovery is thought to contain at least 10,000 billion barrels of oil.
-- EASTERN GROUP IN TALKS WITH CELTIC ENERGY

Welsh open-cast mining group Celtic Energy is in discussions with Eastern Group, formerly part of Hanson, about developing a 400MW clean coal power station. Eastern is part of Energy Group, which is expected to be demerged from Hanson shortly. The group is planning several new power plants, including two further combined cycle gas-fired plants and an unspecified number of combined heat and power facilities.
-- BID FOR CLYDE PETROLEUM IN FINAL STRAIGHT

The fate of Clyde Petroleum, the UK oil independent at the centre of a 494 million stg hostile bid from Gulf Canada Resources, rests with a small group of fund managers. Decisions are expected in the next few days from Schroders, Norwich Union, Capital Group, the Whittington Group and the Prudential, all of whom hold significant stakes in Clyde. Analysts and protagonists alike are agreed that the fight for Clyde is likely to be close.
